# A Novel Approach for Pancreas Transcriptomics Reveals the Cellular Landscape in Homeostasis and Acute Pancreatitis

**Authors:** Katherine J. Aney; Woo-Jeong Jeong; Andres F. Vallejo; Cassandra Burdziak; Ethan Chen; Austin Wang; Pal Koak; Kellie Wise; Kirk Jensen; Dana Pe’er; Stephanie K. Dougan; Luciano Martelotto; Sahar Nissim

**Affiliations:** 1Biological and Biomedical Sciences Program, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA 02115, USA. | 2Health Sciences &Technology Program, Harvard-MIT, Boston, MA 02115, USA. | 3Genetics Division, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA 02115, USA. | 4Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Boston, MA 02115, USA. | 5University of Southampton, Southampton, United Kingdom. | 6Computational and Systems Biology Program, Sloan Kettering Institute, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, New York, NY 10065, USA. | 7Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA. | 8Adelaide Centre for Epigenetics (ACE), University of Adelaide, South Australia, Australia. | 9South Australian immunoGENomics Cancer Institute (SAiGENCI), University of Adelaide, South Australia, Australia. | 10Australian Genome Research Facility, Melbourne, VIC 3000, Australia. | 11Howard Hughes Medical Institute, Chevy Chase, MD 20815, USA. | 12Department of Immunology, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA 02115, USA. | 13Gastroenterology Division, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA 02115, USA.

## Abstract

Acinar cells produce digestive enzymes that impede transcriptomic characterization of the exocrine pancreas. Thus, single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) studies of the pancreas underrepresent acinar cells relative to histological expectations, and a robust approach to capture pancreatic cell responses in disease states is needed. We sought to innovate a method that overcomes these challenges to accelerate study of the pancreas in health and disease.

We leverage FixNCut, a scRNA-seq approach where tissue is reversibly fixed with dithiobis(succinimidyl propionate) prior to dissociation and single-cell preparation. We apply FixNCut to an established mouse model of acute pancreatitis, validate findings using GeoMx whole transcriptome atlas (WTA) profiling, and integrate our data with prior studies to compare our method in both mouse and human pancreas datasets.

FixNCut achieves unprecedented definition of challenging pancreatic cells including acinar and immune populations in homeostasis and acute pancreatitis, and identifies changes in all major cell types during injury and recovery. We define the acinar transcriptome during homeostasis and acinar-to-ductal metaplasia and establish a unique gene set to measure deviation from normal acinar identity. We characterize pancreatic immune cells, and analysis of T-cell subsets reveals a polarization of the homeostatic pancreas towards type-2 immunity. We report immune responses during acute pancreatitis and recovery, including early neutrophil infiltration, expansion of dendritic cell subsets, and a substantial shift in the transcriptome of macrophages due to both resident macrophage activation and monocyte infiltration.

FixNCut preserves pancreatic transcriptomes to uncover novel cell states during homeostasis and following pancreatitis, establishing a broadly applicable approach and reference atlas for study of pancreas biology and disease.

## Abstract

## Abstract

Digestive enzymes impede single-cell profiling of exocrine pancreas. FixNCut uses reversible fixation to overcome this challenge, allowing us to define cell heterogeneity and dynamic cell states during pancreatitis and establish an acinar-to-ductal metaplasia index.

## INTRODUCTION

Preparation of RNA to quantify gene expression in the pancreas is severely hampered by the high level of ribonuclease and protease digestive enzymes produced in acinar cells. Therefore, whereas single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) methodologies have transformed our understanding of signaling pathways and cell diversity in other digestive organs, studies of the pancreas have lagged significantly, limiting our ability to elucidate pathogenesis of exocrine pancreas disease such as pancreatitis and pancreatic cancer initiation.1 Indeed, while revealing new insights into pancreas biology, recent scRNA-seq studies inadequately represent acinar cells expected by histology, and efforts to maximize the epithelial compartment limit comprehensive understanding of all pancreas cell-types and their interactions.2-5

Here, we leverage a novel single-cell approach using a reversible crosslinker to achieve unprecedented definition of signaling processes and cell-type heterogeneity in the pancreas, providing a comprehensive survey of the complete acinar cell transcriptome. Furthermore, as proof-of-principle for transcriptomic characterization of a disease-relevant perturbation, we focus on the most common exocrine pancreas disease, acute pancreatitis. Though acute pancreatitis is among the most frequent gastrointestinal causes of hospitalization,6 our understanding of the cellular and signaling underpinnings is limited. Indeed, targeted therapeutic approaches are lacking and management remains limited to supportive care.6 Given that acute pancreatitis tissue is rarely biopsied in patients, mouse models have been crucial for understanding the disease and a robust scRNA-seq method in this context is essential. To this end, we apply a novel method to a well-established mouse model of acute pancreatitis in which intraperitoneal injections of the cholecystokinin analog caerulein trigger excessive stimulation of acinar cells, leading to stereotypical inflammation and tissue damage that closely mirrors clinical pathology.7 We report the transcriptomic evolution of single acinar cells following acute pancreatitis and recovery, and define a unique gene set to quantify the metaplastic deviation of these cells from normal acinar identity. Moreover, we characterize on a single-cell level the transcriptional responses occurring in other major pancreas cell-types following pancreatitis and recovery, including immune, fibroblast, ductal, and endothelial cells. The single-cell transcriptomic method presented here provides the most comprehensive cellular and signaling characterization of acute pancreatitis to date, as well as a broadly applicable approach and reference atlas for the study of pancreas disease.

## MATERIALS AND METHODS

### Pancreatitis Samples

Acute pancreatitis in male C57BL/6 mice from The Jackson Laboratory was induced at 8–9 weeks of age by administering caerulein as previously described.8 Mice fed ad libitum were intraperitoneal injected with caerulein (0.1 μg/g diluted in saline; Millipore-Sigma) on two consecutive days once every hour for 8 hours. The final injection of caerulein was defined as hour 0. All animal procedures were performed according to institutional IACUC and relevant guidelines.

### FixNCut Single-cell Preparation

A piece of the pancreas was incubated in dithiobis(succinimidyl propionate) (DSP) at room temperature (RT) for 30 minutes. After fixation, the crosslinker was quenched with 1 M Tris-HCl pH 7.5, followed by incubation for 30 minutes in PBS containing 200 μg/mL Liberase TM (Millipore-Sigma) at 37°C. Cells were strained, washed, and then resuspended in PBS containing 1% BSA and 2 U/μL RNase Inhibitor (Millipore-Sigma). Detailed methods are provided in Supplementary Materials.

### scRNA-seq Sample Processing and Data Analysis

Cells were counted using a LUNA-FL™ (LogosBiosystem) and immediately loaded onto the 10x Chromium controller (10x Genomics) to achieve a target capture of 10,000 cells. Libraries were prepared using Chromium Single-Cell 3' Reagent Kit V3.1 following manufacturer's instructions. Libraries were sequenced using the Illumina NovaSeq6000 platform (100 cycles, paired-end). Downstream data analysis details are included in Supplementary Materials.

### Histology, Immunohistochemistry, and GeoMx

Tissues were fixed in 10% neutral-buffered formalin (Fisher Scientific), embedded in paraffin, and sectioned at 5 μm. Sections were processed by hematoxylin and eosin staining or immunohistochemistry. Details are provided in the Supplementary Materials. For GeoMx WTA profiling, two 3 x 4 tissue arrays each containing a ~3x3 mm piece of each time point (n=2) were generated. Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue sections (5 μm) were processed according to the Nanostring Manual Slide Preparation guide (MAN-10150-01). A total of 57 regions of interest (ROIs, 650 μm x 650 μm) were profiled, with 2-4 ROIs selected from each tissue sample. Libraries were prepared according to manufacturer instructions and paired-end sequencing was performed on an Illumina NovaSeq6000. GeoMx methods and analysis details can be found in Supplementary Materials.

### Data and Code Availability

FixNCut scRNA-seq and GeoMx WTA datasets are available on NCBI’s Gene Expression Omnibus and can be accessed through BioProject ID PRJNA978570 and (GSE235874) respectively. All analysis and figure generating code is available on GitHub (https://github.com/nissimlab/scRNA-seq-fixed-pancreas).

## RESULTS

### A new scRNA-seq method improves pancreas cell recovery and RNA quality

We leverage a method of scRNA-seq for pancreas called FixNCut – whereby tissue is fixed with a reversible cross-linker, dithiobis(succinimidyl propionate) (DSP),9 followed by cutting the tissue and performing enzymatic digestion (Figure 1A). Importantly, this protocol is compatible with 10x Genomics’ Chromium Single-Cell 3’ Kit (v3.1 Chemistry).

To ensure an unbiased and objective evaluation of FixNCut, we first benchmarked the method by comparing scRNA-seq results generated from healthy mouse pancreas using FixNCut to other recently published healthy pancreas datasets in terms of recovery of challenging cell-types including acinar cells known for high RNase activity. Using scCODA-based compositional analysis, we observed that FixNCut outperforms other datasets in recovering acinar cells and macrophages (Supplementary Table 1A and B, Supplementary Table 2),2,3,5 and here we subsequently focus on comparisons to the two prior datasets (GSE1802122 and GSE1410173, Figure 1B-D, Supplementary Figure 1A-C, Supplementary Table 3A). Whereas prior datasets2,3,5 recovered 4-19% acinar cells, FixNCut recovered 40% acinar cells, enhancing the capture and study of this predominant population in the exocrine pancreas. Recovering certain immune cells using scRNA-seq is also challenging, however, FixNCut recovered more macrophages and dendritic cells (22%) than other datasets (<5%, Figure 1D, Supplementary Table 4).

To further investigate the performance of FixNCut, we removed challenging cell-types that the method recovered at higher levels (acinar, immune, and fibroblast cells) and observed similar proportions of the remaining non-challenging cell-types (Supplementary Figure 2A). FixNCut detected roughly 4% of pancreas cells as ductal and 5% as endothelial. Low levels of B-cells, T-cells, pericytes, endocrine, Schwann, and mesothelial cells were detected in all datasets (Figure 1D). We also simulated the experimental removal of CD45+ and RBC cells performed in GSE1802122 by computationally removing these populations from each dataset. This further increased the acinar proportions recovered by FixNCut to 54% without improving acinar proportions in other datasets (Supplementary Figure 2B).

The high-quality transcriptomic data generated by FixNCut enabled us to define a comprehensive landscape of the acinar transcriptome (Figure 1E). Consistent with the substantial production of digestive enzymes, protease genes comprised 57% of acinar transcriptional output, mainly trypsinogen (24%), chymotrypsin (17%), and elastase (15%). Lipase genes made up 14%, while metallocarboxypeptidase and zymogen granule/exocytosis genes were 6% and 4%, respectively. As expected to support robust digestive enzyme synthesis, ribosomal protein genes accounted for 4% of the acinar transcriptome, with significantly higher expression compared to other pancreatic cell-types (Supplementary Figure 2C).

### FixNCut decreases dissociation stress

A pervasive challenge in single-cell analyses is the expression of genes related to dissociation stress which can lead to artifactual results and obscure the true transcriptional landscape of cells. FixNCut involves fixation before tissue dissociation, thus it yielded lower expression of genes related to dissociation stress, with less than 1% stress transcripts in FixNCut versus 2-3% in others (Figure 1F, Supplementary Figures 2D and E). Additionally, FixNCut had the lowest percentage of reads from mitochondrial genes, consistent with less leakage of non-mitochondrial mRNA that occurs with damage (Figure 1F). The decrease in technical artifacts resulting from dissociation stress and mitochondrial transcripts not only provides more reads of interest, but also more accurate and reliable representation of native cell states for cell-types of interest.

In sum, FixNCut was effective in capturing higher proportions of historically challenging cell-types, including acinar and immune, more closely aligning with our understanding of the pancreas and with lower technical artifact of stress in captured cells.

### Mapping FixNCut mouse pancreas to human pancreas datasets

We compared FixNCut data to a recently published human pancreas single-cell dataset10 and observed conservation of marker genes between human pancreas and FixNCut mouse data (Supplementary Figure 3A). Consistent with a single-cell nuclei sequencing study of human pancreas, we observed a subset of acinar cells expressing higher levels of digestive enzymes without expressing unique markers (Supplementary Figure 3B and C).11 We found that acinar digestive enzyme expression exhibits a normal distribution, suggesting a continuum of acinar cells with varying transcriptional output dedicated towards digestive enzymes, rather than a distinct subpopulation of secretory acinar cells. Although we observed no well-separated cluster, certain acinar cells produce higher levels of the top digestive enzymes despite having similar unique molecular identifier (UMI) counts per cell (Supplementary Figure 3B and C). Furthermore, RNA-velocity analysis revealed these cells are enriched in spliced over unspliced species, indicating that there is an overrepresentation of newly produced mRNA molecules suggestive of a recent transcriptional burst (Supplementary Figure 3C).12

### FixNCut reveals the transcriptional dynamics of acute pancreatitis and recovery on a single-cell level

To define responses of cell-types of the pancreas to acute pancreatitis and subsequent recovery, we applied FixNCut to pancreata at various timepoints following a standard caerulein-induced pancreatitis (CIP) protocol (Figure 2A, Supplementary Table 3B). Our analysis revealed a transcriptional shift in all major cell-types at the earliest timepoints following the 2-day pancreatitis protocol (Figure 2B-D, Supplementary Figure 4, 5, and 6). Matching histology (Figure 2A), FixNCut detected drastic changes in acinar and immune cell populations following CIP, including a massive influx of immune cells with statistical increases in macrophages, DCs, and neutrophils (Supplementary Table 1C).

We characterized the cellular responses to pancreatitis on a single-cell and temporal level. Following pancreatitis, cells entered the cell cycle, evident from an increase in the percentage of cells in G2/M and S phase (Supplementary Figure 7A). Fibroblasts were the first to cycle after damage, as indicated at the 0-hour point, which has around 40% in G2/M phase and 40% in S phase. Ductal cells and macrophages cycled later, peaking at 24 hours. Acinar cells entered the cell cycle during the tissue recovery process, with the highest proportion in G2/M phase at 72 hours. Following pancreatitis, we observed a global upregulation of genes and UMI counts for all major pancreas cells captured (Supplementary Figure 4A and Supplementary Figure 7B). This may be related to cell cycling during recovery, as a recent study highlighted the association between elevated gene expression and cycling cells, particularly in the context of the physiological renewal of adult organs.13

To independently validate FixNCut findings, we employed an orthogonal approach, GeoMx whole transcriptome atlas (WTA) profiling, without the use of segmentation or masking (Supplementary Figure 8). As expected, the largest transcriptional differences occurred the first 24 hours after CIP (Supplementary Figure 8D), consistent with robust pathohistological processes including acinar-to-ductal metaplasia (ADM). Corroborating our FixNCut observations (Supplementary Figure 7B), the dominant transcriptional change in GeoMx was an upregulation of genes following CIP (Supplementary Figure 8E, Supplementary Table 5).

### Evolution of acinar cells during acute pancreatitis and recovery

One of the earliest and classically described histological consequences of pancreatitis is the metaplasia of acinar cells to acquire duct-like markers and appearance, termed ADM (Figure 3, Supplementary Figure 9A). Indeed, a new and distinct cluster of cells appeared after CIP, notable for decreased expression of acinar genes and increased expression of ductal markers, cytokeratin (Krt8, Krt18, Krt19), Spp1, and Epcam (Figure 3C and D). We identified two phases of the metaplastic process which we annotate “ADM-early” (0hr, 14hr, and 24hr), representing the metaplastic state, and “ADM-late” (72hr and 5day) corresponding to partial recovery of acinar identity. While expression of ductal genes supports the traditional understanding of ADM as an intermediate state between acinar and ductal cells, the comprehensive transcriptome afforded by FixNCut revealed both "ADM-early" and "ADM-late" populations more closely resembling acinar cells, based on the overlap observed in marker gene expression (Figure 3).

As observed by others, healthy acinar cells displayed lower complexity (defined as genes / UMI counts) than other pancreatic cells, consistent with their primary function as digestive enzyme factories (Figure 1E, Supplementary Figure 9B). Acinar cell complexity increased during ADM as cells downregulated expression of digestive enzymes and expressed ductal markers (Supplementary Figure 9C, Supplementary Table 3C). Consistent with an increase in complexity, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA, using MSigDB pathways) on the full transcriptome of acinar/ADM cells following CIP showed enrichment of canonical pathways known to be activated in pancreatitis (Supplementary Figure 9D, Supplementary Table 6A and E). After injury, these pathways are activated in acinar/ADM cells through day 5 and resolved by day 14, and validated using GeoMx WTA data (Supplementary Figure 8F, Supplementary Table 6B). To nominate potential cell signaling interactions that coordinate the ADM and recovery process, we utilized ‘Calligraphy’, a tool that uses expression of receptors and ligands to determine the communication potential of cells.14 ‘Communication modules’ based on co-expression can be determined and used to infer cellular communication between cell-types (Supplementary Figure 10A). We identified an ADM communication module, which had numerous receptor/ligand pairs known to coordinate 1) inflammation, 2) extracellular matrix interactions, and 3) growth factors/receptors, which can support cell growth, differentiation, and wound healing (Supplementary Figure 10B). We identified potential signaling interactions with the ADM communication module that may orchestrate tissue inflammation and the subsequent coordinated recovery of acinar cells following pancreatitis, laying the groundwork for future investigation of these mechanisms (Supplementary Table 7).

### Identification of key markers in acinar-to-ductal metaplasia

We identified 108 ADM marker genes that were upregulated >4-fold compared to acinar cells (Figure 4), many of which were validated in GeoMx data (Supplementary Table 8A). Not surprisingly, many of these genes have previously reported roles in disrupted acinar identity and pancreas disease. Intriguingly, 17 of the 108 ADM markers are known GWAS hits for pancreatitis.15 Pathway analysis on the 108 ADM marker genes reveals many genes involved in cytoskeletal structure/organization (Figure 4B and C, Supplementary Figure 11, Supplementary Table 8C), consistent with the morphologic transition of acinar cells to a duct-like appearance during ADM (Figure 2A). Stress response and chaperone genes are also activated, consistent with previous observations of heat shock protein expression during pancreatitis.16 Furthermore, the expression of MHC class I molecules (H2-K1 and H2-D1) which aid in antigen presentation for immune surveillance, and S100 genes (S100a10 and S100a11) which regulate inflammation and tissue repair, may link cell stress and injury with the subsequent immune response. Analysis of protein associations using STRING17 indicated a robust biological connection among ADM markers (p<10−16) and revealed protein complexes such as S100-Anxa2 and Epcam-Cldn7, which regulate cytoskeletal and tight junctions, respectively (Supplementary Table 8D). FixNCut identified ADM marker genes highlighting the diverse and interrelated signaling processes that regulate metaplasia, stress, inflammation, and repair following acute pancreatitis.

### A gene signature-based index quantifies acinar-to-ductal metaplasia

The comprehensive cell-types and high-quality transcriptomes captured using FixNCut allowed us to analyze ADM marker genes across all pancreatic cell-types and revealed a subset of genes unique to the ADM state and not expressed in other cell-types, including acinar. We leveraged orthogonal FixNCut single-cell and GeoMx WTA datasets to determine a 16-gene signature that is highly expressed in and unique to the ADM state (Figure 5A). Using this signature to score individual cells resulted in a highly specific measure of each cell’s deviation from normal acinar identity (Figure 5B). This led to the development of the acinar-to-ductal metaplasia index (ADMI), a gene signature-based tool for scoring cells and quantifying their metaplastic deviation from the normal acinar state. Following pancreatitis, acinar cells exhibited an increased ADMI score, with a modest but detectable elevation persisting at day 14 in both FixNCut and GeoMx WTA data (Figure 5C, Supplementary Figure 12A). At day 30, GeoMx ADMI returned to baseline, indicating that transcriptional resolution lags behind the histological recovery observed at day 5 (Figure 2A). Importantly, the ADMI validated in independent single-cell and bulk RNA-seq datasets from a variety of modalities and biological processes where ADM is observed including pancreatitis2,18,19 and Kras-driven ADM preceding pancreatic cancer initiation3 (Supplementary Figure 12B-F). This highlights the utility of the ADMI for quantifiably measuring the deviation of normal acinar cell identity following a variety of disease-relevant perturbations.

A majority of the ADMI genes fall into distinct functional categories, including trypsinogens, Reg genes, and ductal genes (Figure 5A). The expression of ductal genes in ADM has been well documented.20 Consistent with canonical understanding, injury led to the downregulation of proteases including chymotrypsin, elastase, and a subset of trypsinogen genes (“homeostatic trypsinogens”), but surprisingly, the upregulation of a distinct subset of trypsinogen genes that are not highly expressed in homeostatic acinar cells (“ADM trypsinogens”, Supplementary Figure 13A). The upregulated trypsinogens exhibited various temporal dynamics. For example, ADM-early expressed the highest levels of Gm2663 (trypsinogen 4), 1810009J06Rik (trypsinogen 5), and Gm4744 (a non-functional trypsinogen pseudogene), while other trypsinogens peaked in ADM-late, including serine proteases – Prss1 and Prss3, Gm5771 (trypsinogen 12), and Gm10334 (mesotrypsin-like). Five of the seven “ADM trypsinogens” remained upregulated in acinar cells at day 14 (Supplementary Figure 13B), findings which were validated by GeoMx WTA profiling at day 14 and resolved by 30 days (Supplementary Table 5). Together, these observations demonstrate perduring transcriptional changes in acinar cells, even weeks after pancreatitis.

The Reg gene family is another class of ADMI genes induced following pancreatitis. Homeostatic acinar cells expressed Reg1, while other Reg genes – Reg2, Reg3a, Reg3b, and Reg3g – were expressed at low levels in homeostatic acinar cells and upregulated during ADM, before returning to low levels by day 14 (Supplementary Figure 13A and Supplementary Figure 14). Reg3a is known to be expressed in multiple tissues after injury,21 which may suggest a role in repairing tissue and reducing inflammation post-pancreatitis.

### Dynamics of fibroblast activation and inactivation during acute pancreatitis

Pancreatitis and subsequent recovery elicited significant gene changes in multiple lineages, including ductal, endothelial, and most prominently fibroblast cells (Figure 6, Supplementary Figure 15, Supplementary Table 3D-F). Given the pivotal role of fibroblasts in pancreas homeostasis, inflammation, and cancer,22 robust characterization of fibroblasts is critical to guide functional investigation in murine models. We first characterized healthy fibroblasts by integrating FixNCut with three independent single-cell datasets from mouse pancreas.2,3,23 We not only identified markers specific to all fibroblasts in the homeostatic pancreas (including Dcn, Gsn, Clec3b, and Gstm1), but also detected heterogeneity that uncovered distinct subpopulations: Pi16+ and Col15a1+ fibroblasts (Figure 6, Supplementary Figure 16). These subpopulations were recently described in a single-cell atlas of fibroblasts across multiple tissues24. Pi16+ fibroblasts are similar to adventitial stromal-like cells and are thought to produce extracellular matrix, whereas Col15a1+ cells are more likely associated with the basement membrane.24 While previous pancreas scRNA-seq studies predominantly captured fibroblasts from one subset or the other (Supplementary Figure 16B), FixNCut identified Pi16+ and Col15a1+ fibroblasts in roughly even proportions (47% and 53%, respectively), in concordance with data from a recent dedicated survey of fibroblasts.24 We used immunohistochemistry (IHC) to validate these fibroblast subtypes (Supplementary Figure 16C).

During acute pancreatitis, pancreatic fibroblasts undergo transient activation with a noticeable reduction in quiescent markers (Figure 6, Supplementary Figure 17). This injury-induced activation was most prominent at hour 0 and 14, where we observed gene expression of known fibroblast activation states – including myofibroblast-like (Acta2, Tagln, Tgfb1) and inflammatory-like (Il6, Il11, Cxcl12, Ccl2) (Figure 6C), suggesting the transient fibroblast activation observed during pancreatitis may involve genes reported in multiple cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF) subtypes.25 We also observed expression of genes that have known roles in tissue repair and fibrosis, including Timp1, Fgf2, Cxcl5, Ccn4, and Il33. Following injury, IHC confirmed an increase in fibroblasts and validated select activated fibroblast markers (Supplementary Figure 18). Activated fibroblasts (hour 0 and 14) were enriched in pathways including E2F and G2-M checkpoint genes, and metabolic processes including in Myc, mTORC1, and oxidative phosphorylation (Figure 6D, Supplementary Table 6C).

As pancreatitis resolves and tissue is repaired, activated fibroblasts reverted to a quiescent state by day 14, characterized by the disappearance of activation markers and the re-emergence of quiescent markers (Figure 6C). Trajectory analysis suggested fibroblasts at 14 hours begin to undergo the process of inactivation, with RNA velocity arrows pointing towards both quiescent Pi16+ and Col15a1+ states (Figure 6E). Thus, our data illuminate fibroblast gene expression dynamics during acute pancreatitis, a highly coordinated process of activation to orchestrate proliferation and repair while preventing excessive tissue remodeling and pathological wound healing.26

### T-cell subsets reveal a propensity for type-2 immunity in the healthy exocrine pancreas

Pancreatitis is known to exhibit a robust type-2 immune response, with increases in T helper 2 (Th2) cells and eosinophil infiltration, but how this disease state is mobilized from the normal immune milieu is poorly understood.27,28 We utilized FixNCut to study immune cells of the healthy and inflamed pancreas on a single-cell level, thereby achieving unprecedented detail of transcriptional responses and heterogeneity in pancreas immune populations (Figure 7A-C, Supplementary Table 3G). Indeed, we observed multiple subsets of T-cells (Figure 7D). Remarkably, even in the healthy pancreas, Th2 cells comprised the most prominent cluster (26-50% of all T-cells). FixNCut captured Th2 expression of Il4, Il5, and Il13, cytokines that have been difficult to capture with conventional scRNA-seq methods (Supplementary Figure 19A). The observation that even the healthy pancreas harbors a significant population of Th2 cells suggests that the pancreas is poised for a type-2 immune response even at homeostasis.

Type-2 immunity is known to be driven by cytokine IL33, creating a feedback loop shown to promote pancreatic cancer, with studies indicating that the IL33 source could be fibroblast29 or epithelial.14,30 Likewise, in the type-2 immune response observed in acute pancreatitis, IL33 has also been implicated in both mice and humans,31 but the primary source of IL33 in the healthy and acutely inflamed pancreas has been debated. Our study reveals fibroblasts as the primary source of IL33 in normal and inflamed pancreas, with elevated Il33 after pancreatitis that returned to homeostatic levels by day 14, findings that were confirmed with IHC (Figure 6C, Supplementary Figure 17C and D, Supplementary Figure 18). IL33 functions by binding to its receptor, ST2 (Il1rl1), which we observed highly expressed on Th2 cells (Supplementary Figure 19A). Collectively, these findings suggest that the exocrine pancreas is biased towards type-2 immunity even at homeostasis, and the secretion of IL33 from activated fibroblasts may amplify this type-2 response during pancreatitis.

Other T-cell populations detected with FixNCut include T regulatory cells, cytolytic T-cells, and γδT-cells (Supplementary Figure 19B), which are a subset of T-cells with innate-like properties. The γδT-cells in the healthy pancreas match the profile of the IFNγ-producing subtype (as opposed to IL-17-producing subtype), expressing Ccl5, Tbx21 (Tbet), Gzma, and Gzmb. Interestingly, these pancreas γδT-cells are Cd8a+ and Cd4−, which is atypical for γδT-cells but resembles γδT-cells found in the epithelium of the small intestine and colon.32

### Transient immune activation during acute pancreatitis: neutrophil infiltration, DC expansion, and macrophage transcriptional shifts

Much like adaptive immune cells, innate immune cells previously observed by FACS33 can be identified and profiled by FixNCut. Following pancreatitis, neutrophils infiltrated the pancreas and persisted until 24 hours (Figure 7C), consistent with their role in debris removal, inflammation resolution, and tissue repair. This evidence reinforces the value of FixNCut, as neutrophil single-cell transcriptomes are difficult to capture. DCs are known to be essential for pancreatitis recovery,34 and here we distinguish discrete subsets of DCs and gain insight into their temporal behavior during pancreatitis (Supplementary Figures 19C and D). We also observed DC proliferation with cDC1 and cDC2 cells peaking at 72 hours, while cycling cDC1 and mregDC cells (involved in immunogenic, regulatory, and migrating programs) were most abundant at 5 days, with DC populations returning to baseline by 14 days.

Recent studies have highlighted the heterogeneity of macrophages and their responses to acute pancreatitis.35,36 Indeed, we find that macrophages and monocytes exhibit the most pronounced changes among immune cells during pancreatitis and recovery, with single-cell transcriptome analysis enhancing our understanding of their roles during homeostasis and pancreatitis (Figure 7C and Supplementary Figure 20). In control and recovered samples, we detected pancreatic tissue resident macrophages (TRMs) including previously recognized subsets Lyve1+ TRMs (thought to be primarily embryonically derived) and Cx3cr1+ TRMs, which exhibit high expression of MHC-II genes28 (Supplementary Figure 19E). We also identified a subset of Retnla+Lyz1+ macrophages in healthy pancreas, which display high levels of Ear2, Cd226, and Lpl (Supplementary Figure 20B) and were consistently captured in control and day 14 samples. Since Retnla+Lyz1+ macrophages have not been previously reported in the pancreas, we validated the presence of this population using IHC (Supplementary Figure 21).

We explored how macrophage and monocyte (Mertk+ cells, Figure 7E) subtypes evolve over the course of pancreatitis as their transcriptomes dramatically shift. Following a 2-day pancreatitis protocol, we observe populations likely to be activated TRMs and infiltrating monocytes (Ccr2+Ly6c2+), with RNA velocity-based trajectory analysis supporting these concurrent processes (Figure 7E-G). Early TRM activated cells appeared to transition back towards the state of healthy pancreas TRMs, while infiltrating monocytes demonstrated a separate progression from hour 0 to hour 24. Activated macrophages and monocytes appear to be ‘M2’-like, as other studies have reported,36 and are characterized by their top markers Trem2+ and Arg1+. Arg1+ macrophages had high levels of M2 markers (Tgm2 and Chil3) and pro-inflammatory markers (Hif1a, Ccr1, and Clec4d), while Trem2+ macrophages primarily had anti-inflammatory markers (Spp1 and Gpnmb, Supplementary Figure 20). We used IHC to validate markers of activated macrophages and confirm macrophage proliferation (Supplementary Figure 22), which peaked during recovery at 24 hours (Supplementary Figure 7A). Importantly, at day 14, there was no evidence of enduring transcriptional changes in pancreas macrophages, and recovered macrophages appear to revert to their pre-injury states.

## DISCUSSION

Owing to its massive production of nucleases and proteases to aid digestion, the exocrine pancreas has been a challenging organ to study. Here, we harness a novel method, FixNCut9, that overcomes the hostile context of endogenous RNases to achieve unprecedented single-cell transcriptomic definition of pancreas populations at homeostasis and following caerulein-induced acute pancreatitis and recovery. FixNCut has been recently demonstrated in other tissue contexts to achieve immediate sample preservation and thus improve RNA integrity and sequencing library complexity9, and here we present the first application of this method in the pancreas. FixNCut doubles acinar cell recovery and uncovers specific subsets of immune cells in the pancreas, including neutrophils, macrophages, and DC populations. Furthermore, we identified fibroblast subsets in the homeostatic pancreas (Pi16+ and Col15a1+) that have previously been identified as universal fibroblasts and have similarities to human fibroblasts.24 Moreover, fixation significantly mitigates stress-response genes and alterations of the native cell state, enhancing transcriptome interpretation and reproducibility. Put together, we provide a comprehensive catalog of pancreas cell-types in homeostasis and acute pancreatitis and have compiled a ‘Pancreas Marker Atlas’, which indexes marker genes as well as cross-references to previous studies (Supplementary Table 9). We demonstrate the utility of FixNCut by interrogating a caerulein-induced mouse model of acute pancreatitis, a pancreas disease for which human samples are rare, providing a blueprint for the controlled study of pancreas pathobiology.

A key contribution of this new method is novel insights into acinar cell biology. Leveraging FixNCut, we generate high-quality transcriptomic landscapes for healthy and perturbed acinar cells and validate previous findings indicating a relatively low-complexity transcriptome in healthy acinar cells. We characterized ADM, identifying genes involved in pathways including cytoskeletal regulation, stress response, and immune modulation. Interestingly, we find that ADM marker genes following caerulein-induced acute pancreatitis mirror those following 2- and 4- week chronic pancreatitis,40 but chronic pancreatitis elicits many more ductal genes suggesting a greater degree of ductal metaplasia (Supplementary Figure 23). While a descriptive state of ADM is well established in pancreas biology, the field lacks an objective measure to quantify metaplasia in cells. Our single-cell data enabled us to identify a set of genes highly specific to the ADM state, which we used to define an ADMI scoring tool that validated in GeoMx samples following acute pancreatitis, across different studies, and in the context of Kras-driven ADM. ADMI offers an easy-to-use and objective standard to quantify deviation of acinar cells from normal identity, and thus a tool that can be applied to bulk or scRNA-seq to measure how these deviations change over time or following diverse insults such as age, metabolic or endocrine derangements, or oncogenic drivers.

Surprisingly, the ADMI genes include a subset of trypsinogen genes that are upregulated following caerulein-induced acute pancreatitis, a paradoxical response that was corroborated in our GeoMx WTA data and a recent bulk RNA-seq study.18 Why a subset of “ADM trypsinogens” are upregulated following acute pancreatitis is not known and raises new hypotheses about the roles of trypsinogens during pancreatitis and recovery. One possibility is that “ADM trypsinogens” facilitate rapid restoration of digestive enzyme reserves and acinar cell function following injury until the normal stock of “homeostatic trypsinogens” can be regenerated. Another possibility is that these trypsinogens have a non-canonical role in resolving inflammation and promoting repair following injury, akin to the use of trypsinogens in an oral solution to promote tissue repair post-operatively.41 These findings warrant further investigation into this subset of trypsinogens to probe their function in the pathophysiology of acute pancreatitis and possible therapeutic implications.

Another group of genes comprising the ADMI are Reg. While Reg secretory proteins have been shown to drive and sustain the ADM state, they also have a role in promoting tissue repair by modulating inflammation and promoting proliferation.21 Others have observed similar alterations in Reg expression in the early phase of acute pancreatitis.42 Notably, Reg genes are highly conserved in human and upregulated during injury or inflammation.21 Human REG3A is expressed at low levels in the homeostatic pancreas and is observed to be upregulated in both ADM and pancreatic cancer.42 Furthermore, in an organ donor dataset, we find upregulation of ADMI genes (REG3A, REG3G, and CLDN4) in human samples where acinar identity is perturbed (“healthy ADM” and “Tumor Acinar”)10.

Our work also contributes new insights in pancreas immunology. The importance of lymphocytes in resolving inflammation is highlighted in mouse models, where their absence leads to prolonged pancreatitis and macrophage infiltration.37 While traditional methods like fluorescence-activated cell sorting have demonstrated the presence of various T-cell subsets in the pancreas, including γδT cells,38 T-regs,39 and Th2 cells,39 FixNCut offers an unbiased method to detect these populations, characterize their transcriptomes at single-cell resolution, and detail gene expression in fixed cells to elucidate cell states and roles during pancreas homeostasis and disease. It is known that disease states of the exocrine pancreas --- pancreatitis and PDAC --- are characterized by a type-2 immune response.42,43 Here, we provide an important perspective on how these disease states arise, revealing that the homeostatic pancreas is biased towards type-2 immunity, with fibroblast-derived IL33 hypothesized to maintain this state and amplify the type-2 immune responses. A major strength of FixNCut is that it captures transcriptomes in an unbiased manner, which not only validated TRMs previously recovered using cell sorting28 but allowed for comprehensive characterization of immune cell-types and markers. Indeed, we detected a Retnla+Lyz1+ macrophage population in the healthy and recovered pancreas whose function is unknown. Comparing top markers of these macrophages to other studies reveals their resemblance to “peritoneal cavity macrophages” which express a unique combination of markers including Retnla, Lyz1, Fn1, Lpl, and Ccr2.44 Additionally, we characterize changes in immune populations during acute pancreatitis and recovery, observing a dynamic response of M2-like macrophages that initially express both pro- and anti-inflammatory markers, replaced by macrophages primarily expressing anti-inflammatory markers that likely aid in injury resolution and tissue repair.

In summary, our work provides the most detailed cellular and transcriptomic landscape of caerulein-induced acute pancreatitis to date, introducing a ‘Pancreas Marker Atlas’ and exploring the biology of acinar-to-ductal metaplasia in detail. Given the ability to capture dynamic cell states and previously challenging cell-types including acinar and immune using FixNCut, we anticipate this approach to accelerate our understanding of the pancreas in health and disease.
